# Introduction

This script uses the tidyverse and tinytable to clean, test, and run exploratory 
data analysis with socioeconomic index data provided by BC Stats 
[@bcstats2026sei; @bcdata; @Tidyverse].

# Workflow Set-Up

```{r}
#| message: false

library(bcdata)
library(tidyverse)
library(modelsummary)
```

```{r}
#| message: false

socioeconomic_index_raw <- read_csv("bc_sei_data_raw.csv")
```

# Cleaning

First, I will get rid of columns that I do not need. The calendar year column
does not make much sense for our analysis, as all of this data comes from 2023.
The reason this column exists is because BC Stats also provides longitudinal 
data on SEI measures. For the purposes of this analysis, I will not be using 
longitudinal data.

```{r}
cleaned_socioeconomic_index <- socioeconomic_index_raw |>
  select(-CALENDAR_YEAR)
```

Now, I will only include the municipalities of interest. For the purposes of
this data story, I am only considering municipalities within the Metro
Vancouver Region and the Greater Victoria Region. As such, I gather the
official municipalities within these regions and place them into the
cleaned dataset.

```{r}
cleaned_socioeconomic_index <- cleaned_socioeconomic_index |>
  filter(
    MUN_NAME_2021 %in% c(
    "Anmore", "Belcarra", "Bowen Island", "Burnaby",
    "Coquitlam", "Delta", "Langley", "Lions Bay", "Maple Ridge", 
    "Metro Vancouver A", "New Westminster", "North Vancouver", 
    "Pitt Meadows", "Port Coquitlam", "Port Moody", "Richmond",
    "Surrey", "Vancouver", "West Vancouver", "White Rock", "Central Saanich",
    "Colwood", "Esquimalt", "Highlands", "Juan de Fuca (Part 1)", 
    "Juan de Fuca (Part 2)", "Langford", "Metchosin", "North Saanich",
    "Oak Bay", "Saanich", "Sidney", "Sooke", "Victoria", "View Royal"
  )
)
```

In the dataset, some municipalities are named twice because they contain
sub-regions or districts. It is important that we give these better
identifiers so that we can be more precise in our analysis.

```{r}
cleaned_socioeconomic_index <- cleaned_socioeconomic_index |>
  mutate(
    MUN_NAME_2021 = case_when(
    CSD_UID == "5915002" ~ "City of Langley",
    CSD_UID == "5915001" ~ "Township of Langley",
    CSD_UID == "5915020" ~ "Electoral Area A (UBC)",
    CSD_UID == "5915051" ~ "City of North Vancouver",
    CSD_UID == "5915046" ~ "District of North Vancouver",
    CSD_UID == "5917054" ~ "Juan de Fuca (Part 1, Shirley, Jordan River, Malahat)",
    CSD_UID == "5917056" ~ "Juan de Fuca (Part 2, Port Renfrew)",
    TRUE ~ MUN_NAME_2021
  )
)
```

Let's also rename the columns so that they look cleaner.

```{r}
cleaned_socioeconomic_index <- cleaned_socioeconomic_index |>
  rename(
    Municipality = MUN_NAME_2021,
    Average_Age = AVERAGE_AGE,
    Population_2023 = POPULATION_ESTIMATE,
    Total_Index = TOTAL_INDEX_0_100,
    Socioeconomic_Index = SEI_INDEX_0_100,
    Economics = ECON_0_100,
    Education = EDUC_0_100,
    Health = HEALTH_0_100,
    Community = COMMUNITY_0_100
  )
```

Now, let's make it so that the index data only goes up to two decimal
points. My reasoning for this is that after two decimal points, the differences 
in scores become trivial for a social measure such as well-being.

```{r}
#| warning: false

index_decimal <- 2

cleaned_socioeconomic_index <- cleaned_socioeconomic_index |>
  mutate(
    across(
      c(
        Total_Index, 
        Socioeconomic_Index, 
        Economics,
        Education,
        Health, 
        Community,
        Average_Age
    ), 
    round, digits = index_decimal
  )
)

cleaned_socioeconomic_index |>
  as_tibble()
```

# Tests

I have two basic tests I want to run. The first is to make sure all variables 
are proper class. I am doing this by using the stopifnot function, which will 
stop running the code if it detects a variable that is not the proper class. 
The second is to make sure there are no negative values in the numeric 
variables. This code uses a logical if/else function to print out either 
'passed' or 'stop' statements depending on whether number less than zero are 
found in each variable.

```{r}
stopifnot(
  "Municipality must be a character" = 
    is.character(cleaned_socioeconomic_index$Municipality),
  "Population must be numeric" = 
    is.numeric(cleaned_socioeconomic_index$Population_2023),
  "Average age must be numeric" = 
    is.numeric(cleaned_socioeconomic_index$Average_Age),
  "Total index must be numeric" = 
    is.numeric(cleaned_socioeconomic_index$Total_Index),
  "SEI must be numeric" = 
    is.numeric(cleaned_socioeconomic_index$Socioeconomic_Index),
  "Community must be numeric" = 
    is.numeric(cleaned_socioeconomic_index$Community),
  "Health must be numeric" = 
    is.numeric(cleaned_socioeconomic_index$Health),
  "Education must be numeric" = 
    is.numeric(cleaned_socioeconomic_index$Education),
  "Economics must be numeric" = 
    is.numeric(cleaned_socioeconomic_index$Economics)
)
```

```{r}
numeric_variables <- c(
  "Population_2023", "Average_Age", "Total_Index", "Socioeconomic_Index",
  "Community", "Health", "Education", "Economics"
)

for(
  SEI_var in numeric_variables) {
    if(any(cleaned_socioeconomic_index[[SEI_var]] < 0, na.rm = TRUE)) {
      stop(
        paste("Stop, there are negative values in the", SEI_var, "variable"))
 } else {
      message(
        paste("Passed, there are no negative values in the", SEI_var, 
              "variable") 
  )
 }
}
```

# Exploratory Data Analysis

Before making any graphs, I am gonna get a glimpse of the data and run some
basic descriptive statistics to get a sense of central tendency and 
variability in the data.

```{r}
head(cleaned_socioeconomic_index)
```

```{r}
tail(cleaned_socioeconomic_index)
```

```{r}
summary(cleaned_socioeconomic_index)
```

The code below provides a table of summary statistics for continuous variables
in the cleaned dataset.

```{r}
cleaned_socioeconomic_index |>
  select(-CSD_UID, -Municipality) |>
  datasummary_skim(histogram = FALSE)
```

## Plotting SEI, Age, and Health

Running this code will print a simple plot that puts SEI on the x axis and 
average age on the y axis for municipalities within the Metro Vancouver and
Greater Victoria Areas. It is important that I plot the data to get a sense
of the data outside of just viewing summary statistics. I have also created
a regression line using the geom_smooth argument, which creates a line of
best fit for y (average age) as a function of x (SEI).

```{r}
cleaned_socioeconomic_index |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = Socioeconomic_Index, y = Average_Age
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.5, colour = "forestgreen"
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = "black"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Age and SEI Scores",
    x = "Socioeconomic Index",
    y = "Average Age"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"
    )
  )
```

Below, I have crafted a more complex figure, which leveraged SEI, health 
index, and population. Examining the relationship between SEI (economic, 
education, community) and health index, I can see a slight positive relationship. 
Understanding this relationship is important as the SEI index does not include the 
health dimension. As such, with more statistical testing, I could potentially 
make claims about the relationship between social well-being and health outcomes in 
BC. The population variable adds a layer of complexity and gives a glimpse
into how population is correlated with both the health index and SEI index.

```{r}
cleaned_socioeconomic_index |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = Socioeconomic_Index, y = Health
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(
      size = Population_2023),
    alpha = 0.5, colour = "coral"
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = "black"
  ) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 10, labels = scales::label_comma(
   )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Health Index vs. Socieconomic Index Scores",
    subtitle = "With Municipal Population Statistics",
    x = "Socioeconomic Index",
    y = "Health Index",
    size = "Population (2023)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"
    ),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(
      hjust = 0.5
    )
  )
```

## Bar Graphs

First, I want to create a bar graph that shows SEI score by each municipality. I
also reordered the municipalities so that they are ordered from highest SEI score
to lowest SEI score. I create a new variable that encapsulates all
the municipalities in Metro Vancouver. Then, I use a logical if_else
function to mutate the dataset so that the rest of the municipalities 
not included in Metro Vancouver are placed in Greater Victoria. It makes
sense to use bar charts for my data because "municipality" is a
categorical (nominal) variable.

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 9, out.height = "85%", fig.align = "center"}
metro_vancouver <- c(
  "Anmore", "Belcarra", "Bowen Island", "Burnaby", "City of Langley",
  "City of North Vancouver", "Coquitlam", "Delta", 
  "District of North Vancouver", "Electoral Area A (UBC)", "Lions Bay", 
  "Maple Ridge", "New Westminster", "Pitt Meadows", "Port Coquitlam", 
  "Port Moody", "Richmond", "Surrey", "Township of Langley", "Vancouver", 
  "West Vancouver", "White Rock"
)


cleaned_socioeconomic_index |>
  mutate(
    Region = if_else(
      Municipality %in% metro_vancouver, "Metro Vancouver", "Greater Victoria Region"
      ),
    Municipality = fct_reorder(Municipality, Socioeconomic_Index)
      ) |>
  
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = Municipality, y = Socioeconomic_Index, fill = Region
      )
    ) +
      geom_col(
        colour = "black", width = 0.35
    ) +
      coord_flip() +
      scale_fill_manual(
        values = c(
          "Metro Vancouver" = "skyblue", "Greater Victoria Region" =
            "forestgreen"
      )
    ) +
      labs(
        title = "SEI Score by Municipality: Metro Vancouver & Greater Victoria",
        x = "Municipality",
        y = "SEI Score",
        fill = "Region"
    ) +
      theme_minimal(
        base_size = 8
    ) +
      theme(
        legend.position = "bottom", 
        legend.title.position = "top",
        legend.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        plot.title = element_text(
          hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"
        )
      )
```

Alternatively, here is a bar graph that separates SEI scores by metropolitan
region. This gives us an interesting peek into well-being index scores by
metropolitan region.

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 9, out.height = "85%", fig.align = "center"}
cleaned_socioeconomic_index |>
  mutate(
    Region = if_else(
      Municipality %in% metro_vancouver, "Metro Vancouver", 
      "Greater Victoria Region"
      ),
    Municipality = fct_reorder(Municipality, Socioeconomic_Index)
      ) |>
  
    ggplot(
      aes(
        x = Municipality, y = Socioeconomic_Index
        )
      ) +
      geom_col(
        fill = "lavender", colour = "black", width = 0.35
      ) +
      coord_flip(
      ) +
      facet_grid(
        Region ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free"
      ) +
      labs(
        title = "Comparing SEI By Metropolitan Region",
        x = "Metropolitan Region",
        y = "Socioeconomic Index"
      ) +
      theme_minimal(
        base_size = 8
      ) +
      theme(
        plot.title = element_text(
          hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"
        )
      )
```

Based on this graph, we can see that SEI scores are relatively higher 
in the Metro Vancouver region than the Greater Victoria Region. 

## Box Plot

Lastly, we can create a box plot to see the distribution of scores across key
numeric variables in my dataset. We will look at education, health, community,
economics, and SEI. 

First, I am going to use the pivot_longer function to reshape my data, the 
names_to argument makes a new column at the end of the dataset, inputting each 
dimension (Education, Heath, etc...) in a separate row within this new column 
for each municipality. The values_to argument prints the scores to each 
respective dimension into a new column. The reason I am reshaping the data is 
because it makes it easier for ggplot to differentiate each dimension. It 
creates five separate rows for each municipality, instead of each municipality 
only having one row containing all five dimensions. I have also used the
geom_jitter argument to show each data point within each index, giving more
context to how the data is distributed.

```{r}
cleaned_socioeconomic_index |> 
  pivot_longer(
    c(
      Education, Health, Community, Economics, Socioeconomic_Index,
      Total_Index
      ),
    names_to = "Wellbeing_Dimension",
    values_to = "Scores"
    ) |>

ggplot(
  aes(
    x = Wellbeing_Dimension, y = Scores, fill = Wellbeing_Dimension
    )
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    alpha = 0.5, width = 0.5, outlier.color = "black"
  ) +
  geom_jitter(
    alpha = 0.5, width = 0.15, height = 0
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Community, Economics, Education, Health, Socioeconomic Index, and Total Index Scores",
    x = "Index Dimension",
    y = "Scores"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(
    base_size = 6
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(
      hjust = 0.5, face ="bold"
    )
  )
```

Based on this graph, we can see that economics has the highest median index score,
while health has the lowest. The median SEI is approximately 55
out of 100. It also seems that education has the largest variability within
the 25th and 75th percentile and community has the lowest variability within
the 25th and 75th percentile. The black dots above and below each box represent
outliers that I should revisit and check.

# Surprises

Based on these graphs, the biggest surprise to me was the relatively higher SEI
scores among people who live in the Vancouver Metropolitan area compared to 
people who live in the Greater Victoria Region. Given that I am from Saanich,
some of the SEI scores were surprising, such as Victoria or Sidney
having a relatively low SEI. The SEI scores associated with the Metro 
Vancouver region were less surprising, with places such as Lions Bay or 
West Vancouver reporting some of the highest SEI values. These municipalities
are typically associated with higher economic standing and affluence.
